title: Understand a Programming Problem
learningObjectives: Extract the inputs and required outputs from a problem statement
Identify constraints, assumptions and valid input ranges
Clarify ambiguous requirements before designing an algorithm
Create sample cases including empty and boundary conditions
Define measurable conditions that establish a correct solution

understand.concept: Rewrite a problem as inputs, required outputs, constraints and assumptions. Identify valid ranges, empty cases and invalid data. Small examples reveal assumptions and become a basis for tests.
understand.whyItMatters: Understand a Programming Problem helps learners create Java applications that are easier to reason about, test and maintain. It connects core language knowledge with realistic programming tasks.
understand.analogy: Treat this concept as a clearly labeled tool: select it for a specific responsibility and check the result.
understand.analogyLimit: This analogy is only a learning aid; actual behavior is defined by Java language rules and API contracts.

explain.narrative:
## Turn a statement into a precise problem

Before writing Java code, rewrite the request in terms of inputs, outputs, rules and constraints. Inputs are the values the program receives; outputs are the results or actions it must produce. Constraints define valid ranges, maximum sizes, ordering rules, precision or other boundaries. Assumptions are decisions the original request leaves unstated.

## Clarify ambiguity before choosing an algorithm

Words such as “average”, “nearest”, “latest” or “valid” can have more than one interpretation. Ask what should happen for ties, empty input, missing values, negative numbers, duplicates and malformed data. If clarification is unavailable, document a reasonable assumption and make it testable rather than silently embedding it in code.

## Build examples and acceptance conditions

Create a small normal example and calculate its expected output by hand. Add boundary cases at the minimum and maximum allowed values, an empty case where relevant, and invalid inputs. An acceptance condition should be observable: “a score of 100 is accepted and 101 is rejected” is more useful than “scores are checked”.

## A practical specification

For a parking-fee calculator, state the input (duration and vehicle category), output (fee), rounding rule, minimum charge, maximum duration, and behavior for a negative duration or unknown category. Only after these details are clear should you select data types, methods and control flow. A precise specification makes implementation and testing more efficient.

examples.title: Core concept
examples.code: public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { int price = 120; int quantity = 3; System.out.println(price * quantity); } }
examples.explanation: Turns a word problem into two inputs and one required output.

examples.title: Practical use
examples.code: public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { int score = 75; System.out.println(score >= 0 && score <= 100); } }

examples.title: Edge case
examples.code: public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { String input = ""; System.out.println(input.isEmpty() ? "No input" : "Input received"); } }
examples.explanation: Tests an empty-input case before processing.

examples.title: API behavior
examples.code: public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { int minimum = 1, maximum = 10, value = 10; System.out.println(value >= minimum && value <= maximum); } }
examples.explanation: Checks a boundary value at the upper allowed limit.

examples.title: Test and verify
examples.code: public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { int a = 9, b = 4; System.out.println("larger=" + Math.max(a, b)); } }
examples.explanation: Uses a concrete example to clarify the expected behavior.

practise.guidedTask: For a parking-fee calculator, list inputs, output, hourly limits, rounding rules, invalid values and assumptions before writing code.
practise.independentTask: Turn a vague requirement into a one-page specification with at least three sample input/output pairs, including an empty and a boundary case.
hints: Write inputs, outputs, constraints and assumptions before choosing data types or control flow.
Clarify ties, empty values, invalid data, ranges and rounding; document assumptions that cannot be clarified.
Create expected examples for normal, boundary and invalid cases before implementation.
practise.challenge: Review a peer's specification and identify missing constraints, ambiguous terms and an untested invalid-input case.
